mappings.note: Orders the whole inquiry arc - observe, model, predict, test and revise - so it sits at the inquiry competency rather than any single outcome; C7.1-LO-5 is added because the final step, revising on fresh evidence, is the one the key hinges on.
Labels X, Y, Z as law, theory and principle - the three-way discrimination of LO-4, tested diagrammatically rather than verbally.
The prescribed order ends in identifying quantities and estimating, which is LO-9's method. Not LO-6: no question is being framed for testing, a quantity is being sized.
Statement 1 is the equation as a compact relationship (C5.2-LO-7); statement 3, also in the key, is using it to predict where an object will be (C8.2-LO-7). The false statement 2 tests neither.

All three true statements are about what Saha ignored, what he kept and what the simplification bought him - the full LO-7 formula, including 'adding or removing detail changes what the model can do'.

The reason states why the ignored detail is ignorable (zero physical effect), which is LO-7's 'why'. LO-8 is reserved for the sibling items that turn on the question asked rather than on the detail's physical irrelevance.
Why one approach is testable and the other is not - the distinguishing half of LO-6. Not LO-7: the item never asks what the prediction should be, only why B's is settleable by evidence.
Both the false assertion (Newton's descriptions as theories) and the true reason (what a law does) test the same law-versus-theory discrimination, LO-4.
The mask diagram is used to name the characteristic that real problems cross branches - LO-3. Distractor A asserts strict boundaries, which is the clause LO-3 denies.

Poor curriculum fit: this tests the order in which the chapter introduces its ideas, not any single outcome. Mapped to LO-7 because models are item 1 and the chapter's own anchor concept; deliberately not given three codes, since citing models, mathematics and laws together would be mapping the chapter rather than the question.

The wrong statement to be identified is about mathematics as a barrier; the three true ones are all the equation-as-relationship claim of LO-7. No unit or symbol convention appears, so C5.2-LO-6 is not engaged.
Baking bread needs biology (fermentation) and chemistry (reactions) together - an everyday problem crossing two branches, LO-3.
The three legitimate reasons offered are all uses of an equation to state or exploit a relationship between quantities - LO-7. The false option is rote memorisation, which no outcome covers.

An analogy that only resolves if the student knows a theory explains and a principle guides broadly - the explanation-versus-guidance edge of LO-4, rather than the law-versus-theory edge its siblings test.

Covers both framing symbols, so it earns the compass codes (choosing models LO-7, asking the right questions LO-6) plus the bare competency for the magnifying-glass half, since no outcome in this curriculum names observation. Partly weak fit.

The answer names three emphases in turn - how models are built (LO-7), how ideas are tested and revised (LO-5) and how observation leads to measurement (the inquiry competency). Three codes here reflect three explicit clauses, not chapter-level mapping.

The answer closes on 'the factors needed to answer a specific scientific question', which is LO-8, sitting on top of the LO-7 definition. Its sibling on chemistry examples gets LO-7 alone because no question is named there.
Asks for one concrete simplified representation (spheres and bonds) - LO-7 at the example level, with nothing about relevance or purpose to bring in LO-8.
Saha's simplification named as kept factors versus ignored processes - the 'states which details it ignores and why' clause of LO-7.

The stem fixes the modelling question (a six) and asks which details are therefore droppable - relevance decided by the question, LO-8. Its assertion-reason twin is on LO-7 because there the reason is the detail's physical irrelevance, not the question.
Force, work and cell are everyday words with narrow scientific senses - LO-6 exactly. Not C5.2-LO-6: these are terms, not symbols or units.
Mathematics as the means of expressing relationships between quantities through compact equations - C5.2-LO-7.
Historical and agreed origin of a symbol - the 'arose from history and international agreement' clause of LO-6, distinct from the SI-unit clause its sibling items test.
Consequence of failing to use one agreed unit system - LO-6. The item asks for the outcome, not for an estimate, so C8.2-LO-9 is not engaged.
Framed for scientists comparing results everywhere, so it stays on LO-6 alone; the trade-facing version of this question is the one that also earns C5.2-LO-4.
